issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event
issues.explanation: The trigger set is not clinically coherent with the validated trauma type of toxic chemical exposure. 'Specific body parts associated with the event,' 'power imbalance,' and 'being alone with women' are much more characteristic of interpersonal/sexual assault formulations than toxic exposure.

issues.item: Triggers: Power Imbalance: Being in a situation where someone has power over me
issues.explanation: Within the Triggers node, the items point to incompatible trauma meanings: body-part cues, gendered interpersonal cues, and power-over-me situations imply an assaultive perpetrator context rather than an occupational chemical exposure event.

issues.item: Triggers: Female Presence: Being alone with women
issues.explanation: For a 62-year-old male bomb disposal technician whose index trauma is toxic chemical exposure, 'being alone with women' is hard to reconcile as a trauma-related trigger. It implies an interpersonal/sexual-threat context that does not fit the stated trauma type and is not supported by the threat items, which instead reflect generalized physical danger/hypervigilance.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
issues.explanation: 'Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me' is difficult to reconcile with toxic chemical exposure, which typically does not involve an identifiable perpetrator. This item suggests an assault/interpersonal trauma formulation and is inconsistent with the stated trauma type and the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Avoid New Relationships: Starting new friendships or relationships
issues.explanation: Avoiding new relationships is hard to reconcile with a 62-year-old married bomb disposal technician whose indexed trauma is toxic chemical exposure; this strategy fits interpersonal trauma or betrayal formulations more than exposure-related PTSD, and there are no corresponding threat, memory, or appraisal items to support an interpersonal-relationship focus.

issues.item: Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building
issues.explanation: Avoiding being alone in a room or building does not connect well to the rest of the profile. The threat items describe generalized hypervigilance and escape planning, while the trauma type and other selected triggers do not suggest solitary settings as a specific danger cue. This looks like a maladaptive strategy for a symptom pattern not otherwise represented.

issues.item: Power Imbalance: Being in a situation where someone has power over me
issues.explanation: The trigger 'being in a situation where someone has power over me' is difficult to integrate with toxic chemical exposure and the rest of the selected profile. The other triggers are workplace and loud noises, and the threat items reflect environmental danger monitoring rather than coercion or dominance. This trigger suggests an interpersonal/control-based trauma theme that is unsupported elsewhere.

vignette:
Kwame has spent forty years mastering the art of stillness. As a bomb disposal technician, his hands have always been steady, his mind a fortress of calm precision. At sixty-two, he was the veteran everyone looked to, the man who could defuse the most complex devices with the focus of a surgeon. But for the last nine months, that fortress has been crumbling. The incident wasn't an explosion, the kind he had trained for his entire career. It was a silent, insidious breach. While disarming an improvised device, a pressurized canister ruptured with a loud, sharp pop, releasing a toxic chemical agent into the small, enclosed space. The acrid smell was instantaneous, a suffocating cloud that burned his lungs and sent him stumbling backward. The chaotic aftermath—the blare of sirens, the frantic shouts of the HAZMAT team, the cold spray of decontamination showers, and the sterile, stinging scent of the emergency room—felt more violating than any blast.

He was physically cleared within a week, but the sense of contamination never left him. Returning to the workshop, a place that had always felt like a sanctuary of control, became an exercise in quiet terror. Before he could even approach his workbench, he found himself mentally mapping every escape route, his eyes constantly scanning the ventilation systems and the seals on every container. He had come to believe that the threat was no longer in the devices he disarmed, but in the very air he breathed. The sudden clang of a dropped wrench on the concrete floor would send a jolt of pure adrenaline through him, the sound echoing the pop of the ruptured canister. At home, his wife Amina learned not to approach him from behind; a simple touch on his shoulder would cause him to flinch so violently it left them both shaken.

To escape the intrusive thoughts, Kwame threw himself into his work. He volunteered for every high-risk call and took on all the overtime he could get, using the intense concentration required for his job as a shield. The long hours kept him from having to be alone with his thoughts, especially in the evenings when the house grew quiet. The silence had become unbearable, a vacuum that the memory of the burning in his lungs rushed to fill. On nights when Amina visited their daughter, Kwame couldn't stand to be in the empty house and would drive back to the workshop, losing himself in cleaning his tools until she returned. He knew this created a distance between them, but the alternative felt impossible. His avoidance extended beyond the home; he cancelled his last two annual physicals, unable to face the smell of antiseptic that immediately transported him back to the hospital, feeling powerless and exposed on a gurney.

The decision to seek help came after a night Amina found him sitting in their car in the dark garage, unable to bring himself to come inside the sleeping house. She didn't get angry; her voice was filled with a quiet grief that struck him more than any shout could have. "I feel like I lost you that day, Kwame," she said, her hand on the cold car window. "You are right here, but you're not with me anymore." Her words pierced the hypervigilant armor he had built around himself. He is here now because he is terrified of losing her, the one steady thing in a world that now feels saturated with invisible danger. He is afraid that his fractured focus will lead to a fatal mistake at work, harming the young technicians who trust him. More than anything, he fears that the calm, capable man he once was is gone forever, and he is desperate to find a way back.
